newsitem.title: GERMANY: Rosenthal asks shareholders to back link-up.
newsitem.headline: Rosenthal asks shareholders to back link-up.

text.p: Germany's Rosenthal AG, keen to forge a strategic alliance with Ireland's Waterford Wedgwood, on Friday urged shareholders to approve measures to allow the Irish group to take a 9.1 percent stake.

Speaking at an extraordinary shareholder meeting called to approve a capital rise and other measures needed for the alliance to go ahead, Rosenthal management board chairman Ottmar Kuesel stressed the Irish firm did not plan a takeover.
Referring to Waterford Wedgwood as an ideal partner, Kuesel told the meeting, "To make it absolutely clear, Waterford Wedgwood is not seeking a majority stake in Rosenthal".
A text of his remarks was released in advance of delivery.

Waterford Wedgwood's financial director had told the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung on Thursday that the Irish group hoped to bring Rosenthal back to profit in the next three years. But he added that this could only be done if the Irish group gained an adequate stake.
He said the company would like ultimately to increase its stake to between 47 and 49 percent, depending on Rosenthal's economic performance.
The German porcelain manufacturer first announced plans for the alliance with Waterford Wedgwood in mid-December, ending several months of speculation about a tie-up between the two.

In that announcement it said it would call on shareholders to approve a capital rise worth a nominal three million marks, without rights attached, to allow the Irish group to take a stake. Its current capital is a nominal 30 million marks ($18.3 million).

A further condition of the deal was that shareholders vote to scrap a restriction on voting rights which caps shareholders' voting power at five percent of ordinary shares regardless of the number of shares held.

Earlier this month, the company also announced plans for a second capital increase of a nominal 15 million marks, to be carried out in the second quarter of this year. Shareholders will have normal rights to take up their share of this issue.
Urging shareholders to approved the measures, Kuesel told the meeting that cooperation with Waterford Wedgwood would be a significant step toward returning the German group to profit.

Rosenthal, which has undertaken considerable restructuring measures to try to improve its profitability, narrowed its net loss to 10.7 million marks in the first half of 1996 from 13.1 million a year earlier.
Kuesel told the meeting that the outlook was improving. Sales had risen two percent in the second half after a fall of 8.2 percent in the first half.

He added that an alliance with Waterford Wedgwood would be particularly beneficial as the two companies operations had very little overlap. The link-up would also give Rosenthal better access to overseas markets, he added.
